item.title: DeepSeek: Overhyped, Not Overpowering
item.description: The hype surrounding DeepSeek feels exaggerated and poorly examined, with many overlooking nuances in the broader AI landscape.
item.content:encoded:
The hype surrounding DeepSeek feels exaggerated and poorly examined, with many overlooking nuances in the broader AI landscape. This piece will focus on what I see as missing in the current discourse around DeepSeek.

Claim 1: DeepSeek will choke out the American AI industry with its superior performance.

The performance of DeepSeek is admittedly partially due to impressive algorithmic advancements such as their unique implementation of Multi-Token Prediction which possibly reflects a company culture at HighFlyer, DeepSeek’s parent company, that is dynamic and superior to any of the large western companies. However, I believe the impressiveness doesn’t extend much beyond that.

The prevailing narrative suggests that DeepSeek will cause AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, along with U.S. based chip makers like Nvidia, to lose market share to “The Chinese”. This is reflected mainly in the mainstream media on all sides claiming that this is the first step in a new paradigm shift of power towards China. Marc Andreesen, a prominent VC executive stated that this “is AI’s Sputnik moment” implying that this will be a complete game changer for American AI.

There has also been a huge emphasis on Nvidia’s fall being "the biggest in US stock market history” and “wiping $600 billion off the company's valuation.” Nvidia was probably very overvalued before this crash and may still be. There is no way of knowing what the actual price should be because so much speculation and hopium is already priced in.

Unfortunately (or fortunately), in the AI industry, there doesn’t seem to be much of a first mover advantage. Once the leading AI company creates their bleeding edge model, it is only a matter of time before others play catchup. While this is true of other industries such as the pharma industry, in the AI industry, this catchup can be extremely fast and “relatively” easy.

This is not good for the industry as a whole because it means all of the investment made to train and fine tune the initial model can be bypassed by any firm with a sufficiently large amount of compute and human capital.

As a side note, this is similar to many firms in China that regularly engage in IP and patent theft from foreign firms. This method of growth is to some extent what has allowed the economies of China or India to play catchup with the West and at times reach staggering growth rates as high as 10% for sustained periods in China’s case.

DeepSeek R1, at least to some extent, took advantage of Open AI’s models in training which significantly reduced the price to train their model. This is possible despite Open AI being closed source because they are able to distill knowledge from OpenAI's publicly accessible models.

The R1 model, at best, matches OpenAI’s o1—but with the launch of the o3 reasoning model, OpenAI has made it clear it’s still leading the race and isn’t slowing down anytime soon.

Claim 2: DeepSeek will cripple the American AI industry with its vastly lower costs

Much of the media has been reporting that Deepseek spent less than $6 million for the entire model. This is extremely surprising if true as cutting edge models like this are generally several orders of magnitude more expensive. According to Dylan Patel from SemiAnalysis however, the total cost of this model was almost certainly over $500 million taking into account staffing costs, previous GPU infrastructure, and electricity costs. The $6 million figure is only the cost of pretraining and was likely grossly misrepresented in the media for sensationalism. There is the question of if much of the $500 million should really be taken into account for the cost of the model if, as a quant firm, HighFlyer already had most if not all of the GPUs on hand for other purposes but regardless, they spent quite a bit more money than many think.

To reiterate, DeepSeek most likely trained their model using outputs from Chat GPT’s API. This breaks the economics of making very large capital intensive models when they can immediately be undercut by other companies. Open AI’s profit to investment ratio is already suspect but this makes the economic models for investment in AI companies make even less sense than before and will possibly stifle industry innovation as the money stream dries up.

This is obviously bad for the AI industry as a whole and will lead to stagnation unless compute becomes so cheap that large investment capital is no longer necessary. An alternative is that the scaling laws cease to be as important and take a back seat to algorithmic advances. And while it is impressive that the DeepSeek team were able to figure out that a smaller, non-reasoning model can gain much of the functionality of a larger reasoning model by training off it, they still were essentially just training off of Chat GPT.

Claim 3: If a Chinese company was able to compete with American companies while only having access to stunted H100s (H800s) that meet the export controls, this must say something about broader Chinese ingenuity or their ability to innovate or at least something about the US export controls.

For starters, the export controls are not as firm as they are made out to be, and DeepSeek had at least 10,000 H100s through other channels, likely acquired before the stricter U.S. restrictions took full effect or sourced indirectly through intermediaries in regions like Singapore, where enforcement gaps allow for rerouted semiconductor sales.

The strict export controls put in place in late last year will likely take some time to widen the gap between the West and China. Their immediate impact is limited because companies had already stockpiled critical components in anticipation of these restrictions.

It was thought (pre DeepSeek) that you need the latest and greatest Nvidia chips (H100s) and a lot of them to be able to compete with the main corporations in the US and that if the US did export controls it would cripple the Chinese AI firms because they wouldn't be able to train bleeding edge models on their outdated chips or at least they would take way too long. The implications of this narrative were that the training of DeepSeek proved this paradigm wrong, that you don't actually need the newest chips to make a competitive model. I see no fundamental issue with the export controls, they simply need more time to take full effect and create a noticeable gap between Western and Chinese AI capabilities.

The recent Nvidia selloff doesn’t add up, after all, the company supplying the shovels in a gold rush will always have a market. Okay, their profit margins might take a hit, but they’re still selling the best shovels by a wide margin.

As AI models become more efficient and accessible, AI adoption will explode rather than shrink. This means that even though DeepSeek may have trained its model for less, demand for Nvidia chips won’t decrease and will likely grow as more companies rush to develop AI models. As Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella put it, "Jevons Paradox strikes again! As AI gets more efficient and accessible, we will see its use skyrocket, turning it into a commodity we just can't get enough of." The narrative surrounding DeekSeek would make one think they had just created AGI and now it's clear that shovels will no longer be important in a post-DeepSeek world but that is clearly wrong.

While I don’t think DeepSeek is ushering in a new paradigm for an explosion in Chinese AI innovation, it has shown what is possible for a lesser known firm to do with not as many resources. This kind of thing may keep happening when new bleeding edge models are released. I don’t know what this will mean for the American AI industry but it doesn’t seem super worrying about DeepSeek specifically. I still think the majority of the world’s AI talent resides in the West and after a couple more years of export controls, the gap between Chinese and Western AI development will likely widen, making it harder for firms like DeepSeek to stay competitive at the cutting edge without direct access to the latest chips and research breakthroughs. As Sam Altman put it, 'we will produce better models, but we will maintain less of a lead than we did in previous years.' While competition is increasing, OpenAI and other Western firms are still driving the frontier of AI, making it clear that DeepSeek is more of a reminder that others can catch up and not a sign that they’ve already taken over."

item.title: Sam Altman as the new Elon Musk
item.description: A take on why Altman is like Musk now
item.content:encoded:
History:

Sam Altman and Elon Musk were both early believers in the modern generation of AI technology. They founded Open AI along with Ilya Sutskever, Greg Brockman, and others. The company was initially founded as a non-profit with the goal of creating Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) that would benefit all of humanity. They have since become bitter enemies as Elon Musk sees Altman as having betrayed the companies’ original purpose in favor of pure profit seeking. The reality is likely somewhere in the middle: Altman perhaps is caught up in the “AI race” and believes that if Open AI doesn’t win the race, other companies with even more compromised values and absolutely no commitment to alignment will create AGI that is even more misaligned with humanity.

Elon Musk and Sam Altman both started out in a similar position almost 10 years ago when they created Open AI. Their paths have since diverged and, in the last couple of years, they have become open enemies on twitter. Musk has also sued Altman twice since leaving Open AI for what he sees as a radical departure of the company from its founding mission.

Argument:

I argue that there is a deeper trend here where Musk and Altman increasingly mirror each other. In the last year or two as the AI boom heats up, Altman can be seen on X, (Musk’s company), hyping up his latest pet project or talking about his predictions for the future of Open AI and AI as a whole. These predictions and pontifications have become more and more exaggerated as Altman attempts to raise enough money to fuel the massive CapEX spending that the large AI companies rely on. This AI boom has progressively become contingent on the ability of people like Altman, Musk, and Jensen Huang to keep the AI hype alive. They have all argued that the money being dumped into AI spending is completely justified and the bubble will not pop. This is despite the unprecedented ratios of investment and proposed investment to profit, and the circular financing going on.

Elon Musk is famously able to raise large amounts of money for his pet projects. For the boring company, he was able to raise almost $1 billion over 3 funding rounds despite making almost no visible progress on the tunnel during that time. He was then able to sell over $11 million in Boring company merch including mugs, bricks, and flamethrowers. SolarCity, another project of his, was eventually folded into Tesla, but not before raising on the order of $9 billion. He has a remarkable ability to galvanize investors to fund his companies. He commands the attention of the people in a way that almost no other CEO can. Additionally, Tesla has been quite successful just spreading through natural mediums like word of mouth and social media because everyone knows Elon Musk.

In a similar way, Altman has attempted to raise money for several dubious companies. He co-founded WorldCoin, a cryptocurrency that raised $250 million but has been plagued by privacy issues and does not clearly even have a use-case in a pre-AGI world. He was also a major investor in the defunct Humane AI pin. This is not to say that he hasn’t had several very successful investments, just like Elon Musk and especially through Y-Combinator, it is just to build an image of who he is.

Their companies are also headed in a similar direction. They are increasingly built on the back of hype and animal spirits. Tesla currently has a PE ratio of 269.72, one of the highest of any mega-cap company ever. The median PE ratio for the S&P 500 right now is around 18. Though Open AI is a private company, it is also betting on massive exponential growth in the coming years. They are currently valued at around $500 billion in secondary share sales, even though they lost about $14 billion on roughly $4.3 billion of revenue in the first half of 2025 and expect to burn a cumulative $115 billion of cash by 2029. In both cases, investors are paying today for a future where these firms grow into Microsoft-sized profit makers, not for what the businesses actually earn right now. The valuations only make sense if the most optimistic stories come true.

Elon Musk has made some wild claims about the amount of CapEX his company xAI will do in the coming years. Recently though, in an interview for the U.S.-Saudi Arabia Forum alongside Jensen Huang, Musk got a little too meta and said jokingly that xAI would be doing a 500 Megawatt datacenter that would cost $8 bazillion-trillion. Huang next to him pleaded for him to “stop that” as he was essentially making a caricature of himself and of the AI industry which relies on legitimacy to keep the money flowing.

Last year, the WSJ reported that Altman was in talks with investors in the U.A.E. to raise as much as “$7 trillion for a project to dramatically expand global chipmaking capacity.” More recently, he talked about a plan to spend “trillions of dollars on data center construction in the not very distant future.” These are absurd numbers that are based in a future where OpenAI transitions from losing billions to earning trillions, capturing a share of the global economy large enough to pay back the most expensive industrial build-out in human history.

Conclusion:

In the end, the most striking thing about Musk and Altman is not how much they disagree but how similar they have become. Both depend on extreme projections and constant attention to sustain valuations that are detached from current profits. Both present themselves as responsible actors in the AI race even as the financial reality pushes them toward the same behavior of raising ever larger sums and justifying unprecedented CapEX. The feud between them is less a battle of morals and more a fight over the narrative in an economy where capital flows to the most audacious cheerleader for their company. Musk paved the way on using personal brand and animal spirits to bypass traditional valuation metrics with Tesla. Altman has adopted that playbook for the AI age with OpenAI. At this scale, the mission and the marketing are hard to separate, and both men are now locked into the same basic path of increasing investment hype and hoping the profits eventually match the story, all the while conveniently forgetting the high moral standards they once espoused.

item.title: So... Where is the inflation?
item.description: I’ve come across two main stories about why Trump’s new tariffs aren’t really showing up in the inflation numbers yet.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve come across two main stories about why Trump’s new tariffs aren’t really showing up in the inflation numbers yet. The first has two moving parts and says the pain is already there, just being held back for now, and that it will eventually spill over into consumer prices.

One part of this story is that the tariffs are being eaten by companies in the middle and top of the supply chain. In other words, firms are absorbing higher input costs in their profit margins rather than immediately passing them on to consumers, which mutes the near-term impact on prices while it strains balance sheets and investment plans.

The second part is that companies throughout the US frontloaded their intermediate-goods purchases before the tariffs were drastically raised. This was done because, taking into account recent consumer sentiment data, they expected elastic demand from consumers which would lead to lower sales if they did raise prices. They would rather wait and see if the tariffs might be lowered to a more reasonable level, and all-the-while bear the brunt of the costs associated. Neither of these were meant to be sustainable long term though. At some point, something would have to give and they would end up at least partially passing on some of the cost to consumers.

These two combined start to form a better picture of where the tariffs are being eaten, but this was never quite satisfying to me. We had been hearing this (perhaps overexaggerated) story that the tariffs would create runaway inflation that would dwarf the high of 8% seen in the Biden years ever since Trump had begun threatening unprecedentedly high tariffs on the campaign trail. This would be the big thing that would wake up the American people to the horrors of Trump era economic policy! Cost of living was one of the most cited issues this election cycle that pushed voters, especially young people, away from the incumbent party and towards Trump. And once people started to see prices go up, they would surely revolt and turn Trump into a lame duck president. It has been a little over a year since Trump was elected, and inflation doesn’t seem to be moving much.

In the 12 months leading up to the election of Trump, inflation was more or less holding steady around where it had been since mid-2023; 2.7%. In around the 12 months since his election (October and November data are not yet available), inflation has gone up to 3%, a percent higher than the Fed target, but nothing out of the ordinary. Additionally, when we compare the monthly rates for November 2024 to September 2025 which gives us a more granular view of the numbers of a specific month, they are both +0.3%. This is 3.7% annualized which paints a similar picture of the trend. So, inflation is just a couple of tenths of a percentage point higher than it was at the start of his term… But trust, it’s coming, just wait a little longer.

The other theory I have heard floated I first saw on Noah Smith’s blog around a week ago. He argues that there are several mechanisms that tariffs can use to affect inflation:

They raise prices directly, and they make production more expensive — that’s inflationary. But tariffs can also hurt the real economy, causing shocks in the system and an increase in negative sentiment that reduces aggregate demand.

So, although tariffs can be inflationary as I talked about above, they can also lower total demand, and decreased demand chasing similar productivity leads to lower prices. But shouldn’t the tariffs also decrease productivity creating an inverse pressure that, if strong enough, could counteract the lower total demand?

According to new empirical work by the San Francisco Fed, the decrease in aggregate demand caused by tariffs has historically put deflationary pressure on prices and outweighed the inflationary effects of more expensive intermediate and final goods, at least in the short run. So, in the short run, though the forces of higher goods prices are strong, the lower demand force wins out. In the medium to long run (about 3 years), however, it seems like the effect is the opposite and tariffs ultimately have net inflationary effects according to a related paper also by the SF Fed. So, over time, demand recovers as households and firms adjust to the new paradigm and uncertainty fades and the supply-side cost increases dominate.

There is no reason it must go this way though as the degree of both the inflationary and deflationary pressures are variable. Trump’s tariffs are unprecedented in their implementation (or lack thereof), and if the uncertainty from the tariffs persists, demand could perhaps lose the opportunity to recover, leading to more extended deflationary pressures and weaker inflationary pressures.

Noah Smith wraps up by simply reminding us that just because tariffs tend not to be inflationary for a period doesn’t mean they aren’t still bad for the economy or for consumers, both in the short run and the long run. It remains to be seen what the inflation numbers will show in the coming years, but there are many variables acting in both directions here. One I haven’t yet mentioned is the strong possibility that the tariffs are ruled illegal by the supreme court. This could force Trump to implement them through a different mechanism, potentially capping them in the low double digits across the board. In that scenario, perhaps demand would recover well, despite his best efforts, as there would be much more tariff certainty for the market to work with.

All that is to say, the fact that inflation has not exploded yet does not mean tariffs are harmless or that their effects will never show up. The research suggests that in the short run, tariffs look more like a demand shock that pushes inflation down even while they quietly squeeze margins and distort investment. Over time, as that demand hit fades, the higher production costs tend to show up as higher prices, and the long-run effect is inflationary. We are still very early in that process, and the exact path will depend on how the legal battles, implementation details, and corporate responses shake out in the next few years.

item.title: Dignity and Seeing the back row
item.content:encoded:
My Starting Point

Over the last year, my opinions on inequality and redistribution have slowly moved alongside my overall economic views becoming more free-market and efficiency-oriented. I’m sympathetic to redistribution, but I’ve become more skeptical of prescribing solutions that would lead to quite a bit of economic distortion and inefficiency.

Bootstraps and Grievance

The morning I started Dignity, I read a Richard Hanania post on Substack. I rarely agree with him end to end, but he reliably forces me to face ideas I’d rather ignore. In this piece, he argues that JD Vance’s politics parallel the worldview Hanania associates with the progressive left, especially the “politics of victimhood.” The thesis is that many on the right, including JD Vance, regularly bash the “woke left” for their self-victimizing ideology. But Vance has essentially adopted that same victimization but for the Rust Belt towns and rural counties he feels have been neglected and left behind.

He presents it as a sort of horseshoe theory where the left and right end up converging on a similar ideology: the victim mentality. He argues that both the victimized on the left and the right essentially need to pull themselves up by their bootstraps. America is the land of equal opportunity, and, for the most part, your economic position depends on no one but yourself. What made the piece click for me is that it mirrors a tension inside Vance himself, between a story of personal agency and one of injury.

Though I have not read JD Vance’s book Hillbilly Elegy yet, I have read some book reviews and I understand the basic premise. JD Vance grew up in Middletown, Ohio, with a population of less than 50,000, though his family had deep roots in Kentucky. He eventually made it out, going to OSU and then Yale law school. He is critical, especially of the younger generation of his community, for their lack of work ethic and “learned helplessness” that have contributed to their present plight. He describes rampant family instability and drug addiction when he was growing up that has only gotten worse, in contrast to the relative prosperity of previous generations in the community. He does not discount the role of globalization and deindustrialization in getting rid of the jobs and opportunities for the younger generation, but believes that if he was able to escape, others can too with enough determination, grit and some luck.

The book was published on June 28, 2016, a couple of months before Donald Trump was elected. At that time, JD Vance described Trump as “cultural heroin. He makes some feel better for a bit. But he cannot fix what ails them.” He even compared Trump to “America’s Hitler.” In the time since, his stance on Trump and his stance on the issues covered in his book have softened significantly and he has become much more sympathetic to the plight of the places left behind by deindustrialization. He began to shift blame from mostly personal responsibility towards mainly globalization and immigration.

Dignity in Work

Chris Arnade’s Dignity offers a different perspective on the state of what he calls “back row America.” He walks around cities and towns that no longer have hope; places like Gary, Indiana, Selma, Alabama, and Hunts Point, New York. Places where addiction and disorder run rampant because there is nothing else to do.

The format offers rich imagery not only through writing but also through photography. The text consists mainly of interviews and conversations (many paraphrased) with members of the communities he travels through. The purpose of the book is to show what the human experience is for these people and provide perspectives that are often overlooked, and it does a wonderful job. I was captivated by the book; once I picked it up, I was unable to put it down and essentially read cover to cover in one sitting.

Most of what I usually read takes quite a broad view of events and people. I prefer to read about graphs and charts and statistics and predictions instead of zooming in to understand what these data actually mean for the lives of real people. After all, facts are more reliable than anecdotes. You can’t make informed prescriptions without broad evidence.

Arnade argues that the problem is not limited to material deprivation; the loss of “dignity” must also be taken into account. In the places he describes, people do not just lack income, they also lack things like belonging, structure, pride, and the feeling of lifelong membership in an organization that will take care of them, things a union job in a steel mill or an auto factory used to supply almost automatically.

I still believe personal responsibility and life choices matter. But after reading the book, it doesn’t make sense to talk about choices as if everyone has the same ability to make the best ones. Making your own way in life is much easier when you can picture a future you are building toward. It is easier when the people around you model stability and expect it from you. It is easier when your environment constantly rewards long-term thinking instead of short-term survival. Agency needs a ladder to climb on, and Arnade made me realize how often I assume the ladder is always there.

Economists mostly agree that globalization is a net positive economically for all involved countries. It raises total output, lowers consumer prices, and accelerates growth, which tends to lift living standards. This is hard to dispute and, if you are a utilitarian, this may be all you need to hear. This was my cursory evaluation: if it increases average total welfare, it is good.

While not necessarily wrong, that logic is incomplete. A society does not experience “the average,” so if the gains are spread thin across the whole country but the losses concentrate in specific towns, those towns do not feel a modest decline, they feel a collapse. And when collapse lasts long enough, it changes the culture and mindset of the people, not because people become worse, but because they adapt to what seems possible. Because of the nature of the jobs they are now forced to take, their dignity is lower than their parents’ or grandparents’. They don’t see the path to upward mobility or making it out because the generational trajectory is downward.

A dignified job doesn’t have to be glamorous, it is simply work that allows you to feel respect for yourself and feel respected by others. Your job is part of your identity and you know you won’t just be fired on a whim so you put in the effort to make sure it is done well. When the dignified work disappears, replacing it with just a paycheck is insufficient. People can survive without pride, but it is very hard to flourish without it.

Community and What I Learned

Community is another piece I used to discount. I used to treat community as a nice-to-have, sentimental preference that people could replace by moving somewhere else and “making new friends.” But the reality of community is more complicated than just companionship. It is a bulwark of identity and culture and a hedge against despair. Two people can have the same income and live radically different lives depending on whether they live in a place with a stable and tight-knit community or one where the social fabric is ready to tear.

This also changes how I hear the classic response: “If there’s no jobs, why not just move?” For people like me, moving can feel like freedom and growth. Changing jobs will often increase your salary and changing cities opens up new opportunities and experiences. But for many people, moving feels like cutting ties with a cornerstone in their life. It means leaving their family and friends and everything they have ever known.

This is exemplified in the book when Arnade asks several people why they chose to stay even after the good jobs are long gone and the town has been hollowed out. They rarely say they love their hometown. Instead, they tell him that this is all they have ever known and it would be absurd to try and set down roots anywhere else when the rest of the world seems foreign. Even if they move away for work for some time, many will return to raise their kids and grandkids as their parents and grandparents did before them. The town was built for an economy that no longer exists, but the people and the social ties remain. When jobs leave, the local labor market can’t absorb the existing population, and the pull of family, familiarity, and community makes mobility and retraining harder than one might assume. Over time, that mismatch compounds.

Coming back to Hanania’s piece and JD Vance, I agreed with the basic critique that the rhetoric of grievance can become a mirror image across the political spectrum. People condemn victimhood until their side becomes the victim. But reading Dignity moved me from thinking of it as a simple parallel to thinking of it as a symptom. When people lose dignity and community, they will reach for something that restores a sense of meaning and status. Sometimes that can take the form of faith, family, honest work and service, and sometimes it can turn into resentment and scapegoating. He treats racial resentment as one of several ways a fraying community can try to create belonging. The presence of the rhetoric matters, but the conditions that make it compelling matter more.

So, going forward, I am trying to hold a more humble and disciplined posture. I still favor growth and markets as a mechanism to achieve that growth, but I am less willing to treat the hollowing out of communities as an acceptable side effect that people should simply “adjust” to. If we want a stable and decent society, we need ways for ordinary people to earn dignity through ordinary work, inside communities that provide stability and allow people to survive and thrive.

On a personal level, this has also been a check on my own reflexes. I notice how easily I respect people who I think are like me: ambitious, upwardly mobile, obsessed with optimizing their future. Arnade forced me to see the arrogance in that. It is too easy to mistake my environment for my virtue. If I care about finding truth, I cannot build my worldview only out of charts and my own life story. I have to look harder and more directly at lives that feel foreign to me and treat them as being just as valid as everything else I read.

item.title: Maximizing Gift Surplus Through the Gift Multiplier and Regifting
item.description: A few thoughts on why giving creates surplus and why regifting shouldn’t be taboo
item.content:encoded:
Why gifts create surplus

The holiday season just passed, and it got me thinking about what gifts actually do. I want to argue two things. First, we should give gifts more often than we currently do, even outside the official gift holidays. Second, we should regift more on the margin, because it keeps value moving toward the people who will actually enjoy it.

Most people don’t weigh the happiness of everyone equally. They would not be willing to give up 9 utils if it meant someone on the other side of the world received 10 utils. This is normal behavior and no one can reasonably be expected to live as if they would carry out this transaction. If we treated distant strangers’ welfare as equal to our own, we’d feel obligated to give nearly everything away, because the world is so unequal.

A simple way to describe this is with a caring weight. Think of it like this: my own wellbeing includes my own experiences, but it also includes some fraction of other people’s experiences. For most strangers, that fraction is small, but for close friends it gets larger. For a spouse or a child, it gets closer to one, or even larger than one in the sense that their joy can matter as much as mine, and sometimes more.

Not only would many parents be willing to give up 10 utils if it meant their child got 10 utils, they would likely be willing to give up 10 utils for their children’s 9 utils or even less. For this immediate family and for some people, close friends or extended family, utility can be multiplied when it transfers from one party to another, even when there is some loss along the way. In the context of gifts in these relationships, I will call this the gift multiplier.

The gift multiplier

When I give a gift to someone I care about, two things happen at minimum. First, the recipient gets value from the object itself. Maybe it’s useful, beautiful, comforting, or interesting. Second, I get value from their value. If I care about you, your happiness feeds back into mine. The same $30 item can do more total work inside a close relationship than it could in a random transaction, because it produces wellbeing on both sides.

When one gives a gift to someone they care about, the paper value of that gift is multiplied by some factor. There are two main channels through which gifts can gain value under this paradigm. In the first, the gift has some value it was purchased for which is multiplied just from the action of giving the gift to the other party. A simple case is cash or a gift card where the object’s value is basically its face value.

In the second, the gift gains value through the labor of the giftgiver. This can be through actual labor such as making a creative origami piece for someone. Or it can be through the thought put into the type of gift bought such as buying a dog statue for a dog lover. It can even be a combination of the two where you pick something that fits them perfectly and then add a personal touch like a heartfelt letter connecting the gift to your relationship.

A third effect that amplifies both and allows a gift to keep on giving is repetition. If it is used often, or placed somewhere visible, it keeps reactivating the relationship.

All that is to say, giving gifts, especially to people close to you can multiply welfare, and therefore, should be done more often, even outside of times like birthday parties or Christmas where gifts are expected.

That does not necessarily mean spending more money. In fact, the best gifts usually are not expensive. Their value tends to come from fit and thought. A cheap gift that feels tuned to someone’s life can beat an expensive gift that feels generic.

The case for regifting

This next section mainly applies to durable gifts which are just a subset of gifts.

Most gifts deliver their sentimental message early. The recipient receives the core signal that they matter to the giver, and, after that, the physical object is mostly just an object. After some amount of time, the person who received the gift has already extracted most of the lifetime value they will receive from that gift. Afterall, “it’s (mostly) the thought that counts.” If a gift is special, personal, handmade, or tied to a deep memory, it should be kept as long as it remains special.

Many times, one receives a gift that is nice but is not especially tuned to their liking. This is a good argument against not giving gifts to people you don’t know too well. A misfit gift can feel like clutter, obligation, or guilt to the person receiving it. A good scarf but in the wrong color, a book you respect but will not read, a candle you appreciate but don’t have space for.

Those cases are good candidates for regifting as there is almost certainly someone that will enjoy the gift more than you. The object is already there and the money has already been spent, so it can either sit in your closet or on your desk collecting dust or be given new life in the hands of someone else. This doesn’t mean you should try to get rid of it as quickly as possible, just that you should begin considering where its new home might be.

For such gifts where the dollar value is on the higher end and they hold their value well, they are also great candidates for regifting as the sentimental value is a lower proportion of the total value. For example, a high-end candle, a quality kitchen tool, or an unused gadget has value that is largely independent of who owns it. If it isn’t personally meaningful to you, keeping it mostly wastes its remaining “market” value, while regifting transfers that value to someone else with very little loss.

Regifting is also environmentally and economically conscious as it reduces waste, reduces unnecessary buying, and can often lead to a better gift in a pinch.

Over time, you may accumulate an inventory of regiftable items just waiting to find their new homes. That makes your gift-giving easier, cheaper, and often better, because you can match items to people instead of panic-buying.

Regifting without being cold

Regifting only works if you do it with basic respect for relationships. Obviously you shouldn’t regift anything super personal like handmade gifts, custom items, or anything engraved. That would be strange and likely not end up being a very good transfer as you derive much more value from the gift than anyone else would or could.

It may be wise to be patience when regifting as you don’t necessarily want people to learn that you have regifted their gift immediately to a mutual friend as they see it perched atop their cabinet the next day. You may also want to err on the side of regifting in unrelated social circles so you don’t earn a reputation for not appreciating gifts.

Next, remove obvious identifiers. If the gift came with a note, keep the note (that’s what matters anyhow). If it is wrapped in a recognizable style, rewrap it. And most importantly, do not treat regifting as disposal. Treat it as reallocation, as the goal is not to get rid of things, it is to more efficiently allocate value over time.

Gifts can multiply wellbeing inside close relationships. They strengthen bonds, they signal attention, and they create recurring reminders of care. If you find something that makes you think of someone close to you or you think of someone and feel so inspired to get them something, do it for the surplus value it creates. And when you have something good that is not quite for you, you should feel free to pass it along with intention and let gifts keep doing their job.

item.title: At least five interesting things from Pakistan
item.description: Rooftop Solar as a Private Grid; The Military is Everywhere; Smoggy Fog; The Plight of Domestic Laborers; The Looming “Grey Structures”
item.content:encoded:
Disclaimer: I am not an expert on any of these topics and these are mostly just travel notes. I’m describing what I saw, what locals told me, and the explanations that seemed most plausible to me after some reading.

1. Rooftop Solar as a Private Grid

One of the most interesting things going on in Pakistan over the last couple of years has been the unprecedented influx of cheap Chinese solar panels (and all the supporting gear like inverters, and increasingly batteries), not to municipal and state governments, but mainly to individuals and businesses. This is one of the main reasons I wanted to go to Pakistan as it represents an innovative household level solution to a public infrastructure problem, or a “Jugaad.”

Pakistan has been plagued by grid instability for years and this was quite apparent almost everywhere I went. Many places I went to, especially hotels in Lahore, Islamabad, and the northern mountains, had recurrent brief power outages throughout the day. Most of the time it was only a minute or two before things came back. The outages were brief but frequent; tolerable for most households but unacceptable for critical uses like in hospitals or research labs. Additionally, this seems like something rich people would not be willing to put up with. That assumption mostly held as we did not experience outages in the rich suburbs of Karachi which seemed more resilient, likely due to private backup power.

The Pakistani national grid has not yet completely stopped buying back electricity from rooftop solar, but the rules around net metering and buyback have taken on a more political hue. The government has been proposing lower buyback rates and tighter terms, partly because widespread rooftop solar changes who pays for the fixed costs of the grid.

That got me thinking about what the private solar buildout is actually optimized for. In a lot of cases, it seems less geared towards selling power to the grid and more like buying independence from the grid. That naturally leads to the battery question: how many houses and businesses are pairing solar with batteries to cover nights, overcast days, and the everyday unpredictability.

And then there is the maintenance issue in a country whose cities have high particulate matter concentrations in the form of dust and pollution. Frequent solar panel cleaning is a necessity; if you do not clean, you are leaving a meaningful amount of output on the table.

2. The Military is Everywhere

One of the other interesting things that is hard to miss is the heavy military and paramilitary presence in all parts of life. There are the obvious places one would expect to see armed forces, like near borders or in areas with higher security risk. But even in ordinary city movement, one might expect the police to be doing checkpoints and traffic stops, and instead you often see uniformed security forces who look more like soldiers than police, armed to the teeth. The line between “army,” “paramilitary,” and police felt blurred on the street. This is contrasted with what I observed in India. Although there was a noticeable presence of armed wings of the state in Delhi, it was almost always just the police.

Additionally, entire sections of each city felt cordoned off or controlled in a way that made the security architecture very apparent. We were often stopped from entering these spaces for a while. They would ask for our IDs then let us go after some time as if they were just power tripping.

The Defence Housing Authority (DHA) serves as the gated-community suburbs for the Pakistani upper class in the large cities but also operates a large network of schools. These DHAs began as welfare-oriented housing schemes for armed forces officers and families, but over time they were opened up and now function as major high-end developers and municipal providers, with rich civilians making up a large share of residents. They also continue to expand, and that expansion is often controversial, tied up with land politics and who gets pushed out.

Many civilian leisure activities are also hidden behind the doors of a military base or airbase. There are large cantonment areas that began as garrison spaces but now function like mixed zones with commerce and civilian housing, often with better services than surrounding areas. Another rich suburb and business area is Bahria Town, which is not formally military-owned but is reputationally discussed as being military-adjacent.

Essentially, a lot of the most orderly and advanced developments I saw in Pakistan felt military-run or military-adjacent, whether directly (DHA, cantonments) or indirectly (private projects that appear to operate more smoothly when they have the right backing). Bahria Town is also a good example of how political protection matters. It has come under heavy pressure from accountability cases and court processes tied to allegations of corruption from the previous government, and there have been attempts to auction some Bahria Town properties through the accountability system. Under the current government, the message was clear: when a big developer loses its political cover, its future becomes uncertain.

3. Smoggy Fog

On two separate occasions, my friends and I were stopped from going places because the air and visibility in Lahore got so bad. One night, we were told that all shops in Lahore were mandated to be closed by 11:00PM because the combination of night time and heavy smoggy fog made the roads too dangerous to drive on. This also extended even into the daytime as the morning we were trying to leave Lahore for Islamabad, we were told there was a temporary hold on all traffic going to and from the city until 12:30PM.

I checked the Air Quality Index (AQI) several times while in Lahore and saw that it was sometimes double the score of second place, New Delhi. But only when I experienced it with my own eyes did it really set in that I was in the city that had the previous year set an AQI record for the most polluted city in recent history.

Before touching down at Allama Iqbal International Airport, I looked out the window and saw dozens of tiny fires scattered across fields outside the city. Only later, after talking with people, did I understand this as crop residue burning. It also helped explain why everyone argued over what I was seeing.

When I asked about the smog, I was often corrected that it was “just fog.” But the more I looked into it, the more it seemed like that debate misses the point. In Punjab winters, you can get real fog and calm weather that traps air near the ground. And if that trapped air is full of road dust, smoke, diesel exhaust, industrial emissions, and burning fields, “fog” becomes a kind of pollution amplifier.

Several people I talked to seemed to dispute that these issues were even solvable. Some people seemed convinced it was simply unlucky weather, and therefore outside the control of the government. Others insisted the real culprit was crop burning in India and that Lahore’s main issue was unfortunately being downwind of New Delhi (260 miles away). While the particulate matter coming from North India certainly must be part of the conversation, to me, it clearly obfuscates the role that Pakistani farmers and lack of enforcement by the government play in the magnitude of this issue.

So, what’s the solution? One approach, currently being used in Pakistani cities like Lahore, is anti-smog cannons. They essentially spray ultra-fine mist into the air to trap pollutants and bring them to the ground. While an interesting and even needed short term solution, there are several issues. These trucks are quite expensive and taxing on already strapped municipal governments’ cash and water resources, and they don’t actually solve the underlying issue of elevated pollutants in the air. Additionally they are localized, so while parts of Lahore experience the benefits of cleaner air while they are in use, those benefits are unequally spread across the city.

Instead, Pakistan could choose to follow in the footsteps of its larger neighbor, China. During the early 2010s, many cities in China were facing a similar problem to Pakistan of life-threatening pollution. In 2013, the government launched a national clean-air push and decided that an economy on its way to development couldn’t function like this.

In Beijing, the capital, the government closed and relocated many high-polluting plants out of the city. They paired this with nation-wide enforcement of cleaner standards for heavy industry, motor vehicles, and coal-fired power plants. Beijing’s air quality has improved massively over the past decade along with the rest of the country, and the city has dramatically reduced the frequency of the severe smog events that once paralyzed the capital.

4. The Plight of Domestic Laborers

One very visible thing I noticed was the presence of domestic labor and attendants nearly everywhere. From one point of view, this could seem like a very positive thing. It provides low-skill jobs with low barriers to entry to people who need just that. It also frees up time for more educated people, especially women, to do more productive labor by outsourcing childcare and housework.

The main reason I think this is a negative, and why I will not mourn the loss of domestic labor as countries like Pakistan and India develop, is that it seems bad for worker mobility in the long run. Workers in these jobs often do not build credentials or skills that translate into higher-paying sectors as the economy grows. It can trap people in the same role for years, even as the country modernizes around them.

There is also the deeper issue of control. Many domestic workers are expected to live, at least part time, in staff quarters, or they may not have real private space. More importantly, their time is not fully their own. Even if it looks like they have free time, they can be called on at any moment. That kind of “free time” is hard to use for studying, skill-building, or even resting in a way that restores them, because at the end of the day they are on constant standby.

This connects to a more pernicious reason I am opposed to this kind of domestic labor: it can be dehumanizing, both for the worker and, weirdly, for the employer. During my stay, there were several domestic laborers at the ready at all times. As time went on, I found myself becoming lazier and more passive as I subconsciously realized I was not responsible for mundane things I would ordinarily do, like bussing the table or loading my luggage. I was told that these actions were “beneath me” and that it was best if I just let the domestic laborers do them. Even when it was well intentioned, it reinforced the idea that there are tasks reserved for “them” and tasks reserved for “us.”

Eventually, I started noticing an internal shift I did not like. I began to think of them as not on the same level as me or my friends, almost involuntarily. After all, I could feel the gap in the nominal value of their time versus mine more sharply than I do with the average service worker in the US. That is the part that scared me. It didn’t feel like I was becoming a worse person through malice, but it felt like the environment was reshaping my thought patterns.

You also see it in the style of service. Workers are taught to attend to your every need and to anticipate what you want. At home and at restaurants, they kept trying to take my plate before I was done eating. It was a little annoying, but it also showed how closely they were watching. The moment there was a lull in my consumption, someone would rush over to clear the table, as if the goal was to minimize any second where I might have to do anything by myself.

One sight that stuck with me was seeing what looked like a personal nanny who was also a child. I saw girls who looked maybe 11 or 12 accompanying families on outings and attending to a younger child in malls and restaurants. I do not know the details of every situation, but it unsettled me. Couldn’t the parents, or an older sibling, do this? I could not shake the feeling that a girl not much older than the child she was caring for had been sent to work inside someone else’s family instead of being with her own. The power dynamic felt especially wrong because it involved a kid.

I think there are broader effects of this kind of labor being so prevalent in society. Upper class kids learn early that certain things are “beneath them.” And if domestic workers are a child’s main interaction with the lower class, it becomes easy for them to absorb the idea that lower class people are simply “different” and not deserving of the same level of dignity and respect.

Not to go all Marxist here, but I suspect this also creates class resentment that can replicate itself. People who spend years being ordered around may, when they get even a small amount of power, use it the same way. That could partially explain some of the power tripping I observed from people with any amount of authority.

This environment does not seem ideal for a developing country. The upper class grow up to be the business people and politicians paving the future of the country. If they grow up with everything handed to them by a servant, they may carry those assumptions into their workplaces and reinforce the hierarchy they were raised with. And on a more practical level, they may end up less agentic and less comfortable taking initiative in ordinary life.

Another part of this equation is the more public-facing attendants like valets, gas pumpers, elevator operators, and greeters. People seem to really like having other people paid to do things for them. So businesses hire workers for roles that look “inefficient” on paper, but the real purpose is to signal prestige and quality service.

And that is why this whole system will be hard to wean off as the opportunity cost of labor rises and more consumers get priced out of these services. It is ingrained at this point. I have already heard people in India lament the loss of servants or drivers as they became too expensive. More broadly, the overgrowth of attendants, from waiters to window cleaners to shadow salespeople, will shrink as GDP per capita rises. The harder question is what replaces it, and whether the people who used to do these jobs get a real path upward or just get pushed into a different kind of precarious work.

5. The Looming “Grey Structures”

The development I saw in many parts of Pakistan felt like it was done plot-by-plot rather than neighborhood-by-neighborhood. Instead of one actor building a whole district or block with synchronized roads, drainage, and street frontage, I saw a lot of standalone 3 to 5 story apartments or businesses connected to nothing on either side but looking as if there should be something there. At first, this appeared to be a coordination problem between developers, but upon closer inspection, it seems more like a land and governance problem.

The streetscape is discontinuous because the underlying land system is discontinuous. Fragmented ownership, unclear titles, and slow dispute resolution can mean an indefinite hold on building on certain plots and therefore, holes. Many areas in Pakistan also have high levels of real estate speculation. Pakistan’s real estate market has a long-running habit of trading plot “files” that turn into something almost currency-like. This helps explain why some places seem built, or not built, more for their valuation than for living as builders are rewarded for holding, not finishing.

Another very common sight was building husks. In Pakistan, there is a name for this. People talk about the “grey structure” of a property as if it is a legitimate stopping point. The skeleton of the building that proves the asset is real, even if the place is nowhere near livable.

Builders themselves break down the cost in this way with the grey structure first, and the finishing coming later. Pouring concrete is an easy and relatively cheap commitment. Finishing is the expensive part because it requires a dependable cash flow and materials exposed to price shocks.

When I went to the North of the country, the same logic was even more apparent. I saw a ton of abandoned buildings, especially in the more touristy areas. Half-finished hotels, restaurants, and viewing decks that were clearly built for a future with a steady stream of visitors.

The issue there is that tourism is very seasonal, so a summer rush could justify optimistic building which is followed by long periods where demand is severely limited due to weather. This helps explain why so many projects freeze midstream or why finished places fail to stay open. Many of those shells get repurposed as informal shelter, for storage, as makeshift parking, or by Chai stalls.

What I took away is that the built environment is like staged capital. People can finance the first part of construction, but when funding dries up, the city is left with structures and gaps that serve as a record of where belief in the future met reality.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

item.title: Reading Mark Carney's Davos Speech: Why Canada Will Return to the United States
item.description: It still pays to have friends
item.content:encoded:
A little over a week ago, world leaders and the global elite convened in Davos, Switzerland for the 56th annual World Economic Forum. Many felt this year was different from the usual talk without action. This year marked Trump’s first in-person attendance since starting his second term. His speech was personalistic, as they tend to be these days, and was displayed plainly for the global elite to see. In stark contrast, Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada, delivered a straightforward and punchy speech regarding the end of the old rules-based international order.

Carney is a technocrat through and through. He spent five years as governor of the Bank of Canada, followed by seven years in the same role in England. His speech provided one of the first very public counterpoints to the current American leadership’s inflammatory rhetoric on the international stage, refusing what he called the comfortable lie that “compliance buys safety.”

Near the beginning, Carney invokes Thucydides’ aphorism, that “the strong can do what they can and the weak must suffer what they must.” He uses it to frame the current moment as one where raw power threatens to and in many ways has already replaced the rules-based international order. Throughout the almost 16-minute speech, he never actually says the names Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping, or Donald Trump. He doesn’t even mention their respective countries except China once. This rhetorical choice of talking about these countries indirectly gives the speech more power. It signals that he is disinterested in personal battles and personalistic rule, distancing him from these other leaders.

Instead, Carney speaks in terms of “great power rivalry” and warns against “middle powers,” like Canada, being caught between competing blocs. The obvious targets are the United States, China, and to a lesser extent, Russia. But I believe treating “The United States” as equivalent to its current administration is a mistaken conflation, and two fundamental realities undermine the premise that countries like Canada should permanently turn away from the United States.

The United States Is Not Its Current Administration

Talking about “The United States” as a monolith increasingly doesn’t make sense in an era of polarization comparable to the 1960s or perhaps even the Civil War era. The U.S. is not the same thing as the current administration.

The world functions more on good will and good relationships within and between countries than many people think, and less on hard laws and enforcement. The system works precisely because the most powerful actor chooses not to fully exploit its position. Because of the US’s position as the preeminent power since World War II, it has had access to enormous power. But prior to the current era, the vast majority of this power went unrealized.

Small-l liberal presidents before him exercised relative caution when using economic or political leverage, what scholars call “weaponized interdependence,” to coerce other nations. This is not to excuse American interventionism or the many cases where the U.S. pursued its own interests under the guise of global good, from Vietnam to Iraq to countless covert operations. But even these interventions, however misguided or self-serving, were generally justified through appeals to liberal values, international norms, or multilateral cooperation. The distinction in rhetoric is important because it acknowledges the importance of the rules-based order, even while violating it.

The current era represents a stark departure from that rhetoric. Now, leveraging America’s economic position explicitly for the gain of the current administration rather than any broader principle is the norm, not the exception. But this is not a permanent feature of American foreign policy.

This is not Russia, where Putin has removed term limits and entrenched himself indefinitely. Trump’s power is inherently temporary. The continuity between U.S. administrations does not have to be and will likely not be strong. The Constitution is baked into the fabric of the United States, and while it faces challenges, it will take more than a single administration to take it down.

The current moment is but a blip on the long march of American progress. Yes, the current regime demonstrates how much can change from one administration to the next, but things will likely return to a more stable equilibrium. Some policies, like export controls, carry over from one administration to the next more than one might expect, but the U.S. system’s fundamental nature remains democratic and not personalistic.

Pragmatism Means Re-engagement

This brings us to the central tension in Carney’s speech. He presents himself as a hard-nosed pragmatist willing to engage economically with countries that don’t share Canadian values. The implicit reference here is to China, a country with an authoritarian government that Canada would nevertheless trade with. Yet if he truly embraces this pragmatism, the logic points back toward the United States once this administration ends.

They will come back to U.S. because, as the saying goes, “it pays to have friends.” The U.S. remains the preeminent global power and Canada’s closest neighbor, ally, and trading partner. When Canada sees that the U.S. is back to business as usual, it will try to re-establish lucrative trade and defense partnerships because it wants economic prosperity. These partnerships may take on new forms with Canada playing a more active role, but there remains a fundamental tradeoff between decreased integration with the U.S. and economic growth.

Canada may become closer to China, but China is much more likely to consistently leverage its strategic position against its partners, as it already does. Xi may be seen as a more reliable ally committed to doing business, but he is fundamentally playing the same game being played in the U.S. right now, just with a much longer time horizon. The U.S. remains the better option.

Revenge is not a good long-run economic plan, and I’m sure Carney, an economist, understands that well.

What Does Carney Want?

Given these economic realities, why deliver such a forceful speech now? I think it’s at least partially posturing. Carney wants to show that Canada will not be pushed around, and that if it continues to be, it has options other than the U.S. It’s a necessary signal at the moment. But Carney doesn’t truly decry globalization, he opposes weaponized interdependence, the specific practice of using economic ties as coercive tools. He begins to outline what he would like to see: a new global order where middle powers remain integrated but are less vulnerable to manipulation by great powers.

For the majority of countries, globalization has been indispensable to their development. The question is not whether to abandon it, but how to make it more resilient against the kind of transactional, personalistic leadership currently on display.

When this period of transactional leadership ends, and a more traditional American approach returns, Canada and other middle powers will find that pragmatism and prosperity still point toward partnership with the United States. The emperor may have no clothes today, but the republic still has its institutions.

item.title: From Saving the World to Paying the Mortgage
item.description: Some somewhat disjointed thoughts on idealism, adulthood, and value drift
item.content:encoded:
The “grown-up” story

A common refrain heard from “grown-ups” is that when they were young, they were idealists and they all wanted to save the world. Then life hit them and they realized they couldn’t, and they settled into a quiet suburban life.1 The line usually comes with a tone that is half pity, half longing for that time when they still had that spark in them to change the world. They see the loss of idealism as a law of nature rather than a conscious choice anyone made.

I used to hear that and file it away as something that happened to people that were never all that committed to begin with. People that were always going to wash out; but nothing like me. I was a real salt of the earth anarcho-communist and would remain one until I was Noam Chomsky’s age. I have watched other people describe the same arc in their own language: “I used to be like that as well, then I grew up and realized it’s not practical.” I read quotes like, “If at age 20 you are not a Communist then you have no heart. If at age 30 you are not a Capitalist then you have no brains.” I then proceeded to grow up, understand the world better, and become a free market capitalist.

That is the crude version of the arc. The more honest version is that I did not stop caring about morality. I ran into the fact that the world has constraints, that incentives are real, that systems do not forgive wishful thinking, and that some ideologies sound more moral because they let you skip the part where they actually have to work in practice. The hardest part of growing up is not learning that you cannot save the world alone. The hardest part is noticing the point where “I can’t do everything” becomes “I will do nothing,” or “I will do something small and then give myself permission to stop thinking about it.”

The comfort of theory

A couple of years ago I flirted with communism. It was during COVID, when my ideas could run wild and unchecked. But it felt real. It felt like the first real thing I had learned about. The first thing that really resonated on a deep level. I wanted to believe that this ideology was true and practical because it seemed morally good. Therefore, I turned a blind eye to the minutiae and filled in the holes that didn’t seem to make sense with “I just don’t know enough yet.” The thing is, it needs to make sense.

Like every young aspiring leftist, I always felt like I didn’t read enough theory. Theory is the only thing you can grab on to because there is no practice. There is no case of communism working so phenomenally well that one can use it as a north star. It can be easy to get lost in the world of theory because it is convenient.

I think about that period in my life quite a bit, not because I want to reopen the communism bag of worms, but because it taught me something general, that when practice is absent or uncomfortable, theory becomes an easy escape. It is cleaner than reality and it feels like progress when it’s really just motion.

And that is the part that matters for the rest of this essay, because it is not a communist-specific failure mode, but a very generally human one. It shows up anywhere there is a moral project big enough to swallow up your life.

EA and the coherence problem

I’m not telling this story to dunk on communism, I’m telling it because it taught me a general lesson that matters for effective altruists (EAs). A simple rebuttal to the “people grow out of idealism” story is that plenty of older, intelligent people remain idealists (see Chomsky). But that rebuttal doesn’t prove what it feels like it proves. The fact that there are smart older EAs and smart older Marxists should make us hesitate before we treat any ideology as something you “graduate into” once you’ve learned enough and matured enough. In effective altruism we are idealists, but we nominally accept that our impact will be marginal and are content, for the time being, to maximize our impact, however small.

EA asks for coherence between what you say you value and what you actually do with your time, money, career, and attention. That demand is part of what makes it attractive, and it is also what makes it psychologically unstable. Most ideologies do not force you to stare at the gap between your ethics and your lifestyle quite so directly. EA does, and you cannot stare at that gap forever without either changing your life or changing your story about your life.

The real implications of EA

People often remark that effective altruism is not tangible and this is one of its unfortunate flaws. You don’t actually get to see the people’s lives you are helping to improve. For me, though, it feels very tangible.

Just recently, I got unexpectedly emotional while journaling about the implications of effective altruism and what my commitment to it actually demands. I imagined the purchase of a new car. Let’s say it costs $25,000. You have the option to either buy the car, or save around five children’s lives in expectation. This may sound extreme, but before I knew it, I was on the verge of tears. How can one possibly choose that car over the lives of five children?

One justification is that you are investing in yourself. “This new car will allow me to be more productive with my time and make more money that can be donated at a future point.” But then that hypothetical future point rolls around, and suddenly it’s time to buy a new phone, because the current one is running slow and therefore wasting time that could instead be put to use doing something productive. This can easily become recursive as you find yourself investing in yourself so much that there seems to be nothing left to donate.

The reality is that the “perfect” EA lifestyle is almost impossible to live. There is a well-known example inside EA of people trying to run the “maximum sacrifice” program and discovering that it turns your life into a constant audit. Julia Wise, who has been a prominent voice in the community, wrote explicitly about burnout and self-care, including the kind of decision that sounds noble in theory but is damaging in practice, like cashing out vacation days to donate instead of taking them to actually rest. Her husband Jeff Kaufman also publicly documented the frugality aspect of this, tracking expenses and treating thrift itself as a tool for increased giving. If your moral identity turns you into the person who never lets themselves off the hook, you either eventually break, or you quietly stop being that person.

One can’t live a life constantly thinking like this, especially not with a family. But when you think about the impact your money could be having, it becomes very hard to morally justify large purchases because they so plainly and obviously come at the cost of lives you could have improved, suffering you could have reduced, or potentially catastrophic futures you could have marginally helped to prevent. But are small purchases any better just because they don’t feel like a consequential decision, or just because you can hide them inside the noise of everyday spending and necessity?

Despite none of us being perfect, we must strive to do our best to be, in order to maximize the coherence between the ideology we profess, utilitarianism, and our actions. It is inherently unstable, and a big reason why it is necessary that we continue to update and question our beliefs throughout our lives. There may be no light at the end of the tunnel in terms of certainty for us, and maybe that’s fine.

Planning vs action

There’s also the question of how much time to devote to the planning stage versus the action stage. The optimal amount of planning is obviously non-zero, but it cannot crowd out the amount of time spent acting.

This is the failure mode of analysis paralysis. In EA it shows up as a more respectable version of this concept. Because the planning is not random but rigorous, it feels like more can always be done. You can always justify spending more time expounding and thinking about what the most pertinent issues facing humanity are, because the stakes are so high.

Is AI safety the priority because the downside risk is negative infinity utility? Or is shrimp welfare the most pressing problem because the scale is so vast? Like Buridan’s ass, maybe we become paralyzed for a time trying to decide which direction to go in. It can be overwhelming and demoralizing, and could lead many away from the cause in the long run.

One could argue that action is so much more important than theory because theory without action has no results, while action without theory has very real results. But I don’t want to fall into the trap of thinking there is a dichotomy here. In the case of effective altruism, the theory goes that you can increase your expected effects on the world by quite a bit just by finding a more effective cause area or more effective means of implementation in a given cause area. This difference is materially important and should not be discounted. Because there’s so much to do in the world and we are only endowed with finite resources, we must strive to contribute as effectively as possible.

The problem is that the same mechanism that makes EA powerful also makes it uniquely good at producing elegant reasons to delay action. If you are already vulnerable to using theory as refuge, EA can hand you that refuge on a silver platter.

Practicality and value drift

I find myself thinking about the arc of life a lot, both for myself and for those around me. If you take expected value seriously, the biggest threat is not that you choose the wrong cause area right now, it’s that you experience value drift over time and stop living like the thing matters. The reality is that it’s extremely hard to predict. I don’t know who I might meet tomorrow and how they might change my life, or me theirs. Will I become a more coherent EA or religionist, or will I reach a crossroads where I pick another path. Will I become more coherent or less coherent with my nominal ideology as life and “practicality” gets in the way. Will some other ideology intrigue me enough to shift my focus away from the beliefs I currently ascribe to. How do I know that my marginal action has an actual impact in expectation?

This is where that grown-up line sounds more like a warning than wisdom: “It’s not practical.” “These ideas are great when you’re young.” “I’m glad you want to save the world, but when you get to be my age, you realize that you can’t be the person who saves it, and you stop living like you’re trying.” If I am worried about expected value from the standpoint of right now, I should be worried about value drift.

My motivation to do things in life ebbs and flows like a tide washing in and out periodically, and it’s not obvious to me that there are not larger cycles in life where the variance is very large. When I look back on the me of just a couple of years ago, I feel entirely different. Yes, an important part of life is change and growth, and I feel like I have experienced a wealth of that, but who’s to say I won’t do another 180° turn and end up on something completely different. If I trust myself at least a little bit, I trust that wherever I end up pointing, on average, will be a better direction than the past, but who’s to say? Not me, I’m no oracle.

Rubber to the road

There’s something about actually donating real money with a real opportunity cost that forces the ideology out of your head and into your life. It is also where you find out whether you are serious, because it is where you discover how creative you can be at constructing respectable delays. You could argue that you should actually invest money instead of donating it depending on how you value current donation over future donation. Assuming equities compound at something like ~8% annualized in the medium to long run, it becomes quite easy to build a very rational-sounding case for waiting until you are more certain, more stable, more established, more practical.

Then come the adult questions. What if the job I find myself in in the long run is fulfilling, fun, and also somewhat ineffective? What if I am unable to tear myself away from this job that I love and end up being much less effective over my career than I would like to be? What if I end up in the heart of the bureaucracy and end up having no measurable positive effect on the world? What if I never end up donating because I always push it off citing the crushing weight of my student loan debt? I would like to think I’m different, as everyone does, and that I will constantly be moving forward. But that could easily just be base rate neglect, the idea that you ignore what usually happens and assume you’ll be the exception.

Analogy to faith

This sounds a lot like how many people describe their relationship with their religion and God: we are continually tested, and belief can strengthen or thin out depending on what life is asking of you. The ultimate faith remains a constant, but sometimes you question if God is even real or not. For some this culminates in leaving their religion behind. For others, they emerge on the other side with even stronger belief, and the knowledge that if that didn’t bring them down, not much can. Whether someone treats EA as one commitment among many or as the core moral project of their life, the question is the same: what keeps a demanding belief system from drifting off base when motivation drops and practicality takes over?

Final thoughts

I partially wrote this essay to the me of the future that is considering taking a different path in life. If I won’t even give credence to my own word, then whose will I give it to?

I often think about the idea of taking the Giving What We Can pledge, where you commit to giving away 10% of your lifetime income to effective charities, like an EA tithe. This would serve a dual purpose: it would tie my hands, ensuring that I am donating consistently, and also allow me to compartmentalize donation, ensuring it doesn’t become an all-consuming part of my life and, by extension, serving as a bulwark against burnout. If value drift is the default and respectable delays are endless, then a pledge is a way of turning this from a mood into a constraint, a choice I don’t have to renegotiate every time I want a new excuse.
